title: Given a string s and a list of words all of the same length, find all starting indices in s of substrings that are a concatenation of every word exactly once in any order. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge 4: Words Concatenation (Substring with Concatenation of All Words)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for every start index in a source string where a substring is formed by concatenating all words from a list exactly once, in any order, with no characters in between, given that all words share the same fixed length. It is solved with a sliding window that advances in units of one word length, maintaining a count of words seen inside the window against the required word counts and shrinking when a word repeats too often or an unknown word appears. It runs in linear time relative to the source length times the word length.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a settlement message is valid only if it contains an exact set of three-character instruction codes, each required a certain number of times, laid end to end with nothing in between. Rajesh scans a long message tape, stepping three characters at a time, and wants every position where a run of consecutive codes uses exactly the required multiset of instructions. He slides a window measured in whole codes, adding codes on the right and dropping codes on the left whenever a code appears too many times.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a window in whole-word steps, tracking word counts against the requirement, and record each start where every word appears exactly the required number of times.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for every start index in a source string where a substring is formed by concatenating all words from a list exactly once, in any order, with no characters in between, given that all words share the same fixed length. It is solved with a sliding window that advances in units of one word length, maintaining a count of words seen inside the window against the required word counts and shrinking when a word repeats too often or an unknown word appears. It runs in linear time relative to the source length times the word length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a settlement message is valid only if it contains an exact set of three-character instruction codes, each required a certain number of times, laid end to end with nothing in between. Rajesh scans a long message tape, stepping three characters at a time, and wants every position where a run of consecutive codes uses exactly the required multiset of instructions. He slides a window measured in whole codes, adding codes on the right and dropping codes on the left whenever a code appears too many times.

**One line to remember:** Slide a window in whole-word steps, tracking word counts against the requirement, and record each start where every word appears exactly the required number of times.

sections.s2_technical:
Let the word length be L, the number of words be count, and the total concatenation length be totalLen equal to L times count. We first build a requirement map from each word to how many times it must appear. The core idea is that any valid substring is exactly totalLen long and consists of count back-to-back chunks of length L, each of which must be one of the required words, and the multiset of chunks must match the requirement exactly.

To use a single sliding window efficiently we run the window L separate times, once for each possible offset from zero to L minus one, because word boundaries only align on multiples of L from a given start. For a fixed offset we move a right boundary forward in steps of L, extracting the L-length chunk at each step. We keep a seen map of words currently in the window and a left boundary also moving in steps of L. If the chunk is not a required word, we clear the window entirely and restart the left boundary just past it. If it is required, we add it to the seen map, and while its seen count exceeds its required count we drop words from the left, decrementing their seen counts and advancing the left boundary by L, until the offending word is back within its required count.

After each addition, if the window now spans exactly count words, meaning the span from left to the current position equals totalLen, we have a valid concatenation and record the left boundary as a start index, then we slide the window forward by one word from the left to keep searching. For example the valid check is `if ((right - left) / L == wordCount) { starts.add(left); /* drop one word from left */ }`. The senior-level nuance is running the window per offset so that each character is visited a constant number of times across all offsets, which is what keeps the total work linear in the source length multiplied by the fixed word length.

The time complexity is O(s times L) where s is the source length and L is the word length, because for each of the L offsets the window traverses the source in word steps and each word comparison costs L. The space complexity is O(count times L) for the requirement and seen maps. This per-offset word-stepped window is the standard approach for the concatenation-of-all-words problem.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the settlement gateway receives raw instruction messages that are long strings of fixed-length three-character instruction codes laid end to end. A message is considered a complete settlement batch only if some contiguous run of codes contains an exact required multiset of instructions, for example the codes DEB, CRD, and FEE each exactly once, concatenated with nothing between them. The gateway wants every start position in the message where such a complete batch begins, because each marks a batch boundary to process. This is exactly the words-concatenation problem.

Problem 2 — Testing every position by re-parsing the whole required length each time is wasteful at the gateway's message throughput. The per-offset word-stepped sliding window reuses work across positions and finds all batch starts in a pass proportional to the message length times the small fixed code length, which keeps the gateway responsive.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `SettlementMessageScanner` service with a `findBatchStarts` method implementing the per-offset word-stepped window, and a runnable `WordsConcatenationDemo` main class that scans Rajesh's and Priya's instruction messages for the required code multiset, logging matches at fine level and the final list of start indices at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's message "DEBCRDFEEXYZ" with required codes DEB, CRD, FEE, each needed once. The word length L is 3, the count is 3, so the total length is 9. The need map is DEB to 1, CRD to 1, FEE to 1.

We run the window for offset 0 first. The left boundary starts at 0, the seen map is empty, and seen words is 0.

Step 1: Right at index 0, chunk is characters 0 to 2, "DEB". It is required, seen DEB becomes 1 which is within quota, seen words becomes 1. Window spans one word, not yet three.

Step 2: Right at index 3, chunk is characters 3 to 5, "CRD". Required, seen CRD becomes 1, seen words becomes 2. Not yet three.

Step 3: Right at index 6, chunk is characters 6 to 8, "FEE". Required, seen FEE becomes 1, seen words becomes 3, which equals the count. The window from left 0 to right 8 is a complete batch of length 9, so we record start index 0. We then slide forward by one word: drop the left word "DEB", seen DEB drops to 0, seen words drops to 2, left moves to 3.

Step 4: Right at index 9, chunk is characters 9 to 11, "XYZ". It is not a required code, so we clear the window, reset seen words to 0, and move left to 12. No more full chunks fit.

Offsets 1 and 2 produce no valid batches because the chunks there do not line up with the required codes.

The only complete batch start for Rajesh is index 0, where "DEBCRDFEE" uses each required code exactly once.

```
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001) message=DEBCRDFEEXYZ
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Complete batch starts at index 0
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Batch starts in message for required codes = [0]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar batch starts = [0]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Batch starts in message for required codes = []
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma batch starts = []
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: message "DEBCRDFEEXYZ", codes [DEB,CRD,FEE] (L=3, count=3, total=9)
    │
    ▼
  SettlementMessageScanner.findBatchStarts()  offset loop 0..2
    │ need{DEB:1,CRD:1,FEE:1}
    │  offset=0: left=0, seen={}, seenWords=0
    │
    ├─ right=0 "DEB" need seen{DEB:1} words1
    ├─ right=3 "CRD" need seen{+CRD} words2
    ├─ right=6 "FEE" need seen{+FEE} words3==count start 0
    │         slide: drop DEB words2 left=3
    └─ right=9 "XYZ" not needed → clear window, left=12
    │  offset=1,2: no aligned valid batches
    │
    ▼
  Output: [0]  (batch "DEB|CRD|FEE" begins at index 0)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for every start index in a source string where a substring is exactly the concatenation of all words from a list, each used once, in any order, given that all words share the same length, and I solve it with a sliding window that steps in whole-word units in linear time relative to the source length times the word length. The key structural fact is that any valid substring is exactly the total length of all words concatenated and consists of back-to-back chunks each the size of one word, so I think in terms of words rather than characters.

Because word boundaries from a given start only land on multiples of the word length, I run the window once for each possible offset from zero up to the word length minus one. For a fixed offset I move the right boundary forward one word at a time, extracting each chunk. If a chunk is not a required word I clear the window and restart past it; if it is required I add it to a seen map and, while it exceeds its required count, I drop words from the left until it is back within quota. When the window spans exactly the required number of words I record the left boundary as a start index and slide forward by one word to keep searching.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the settlement gateway. Raw instruction messages were long strings of fixed-length three-character instruction codes laid end to end, and a message contained a complete settlement batch wherever a contiguous run of codes used an exact required multiset of instructions. We located every start position where such a batch began so the downstream processor could carve out and settle each batch. The per-offset word-stepped window reused work across positions and found all batch starts in a pass proportional to the message length times the small fixed code length.

The senior-level point I make is that running the window per offset is what keeps the work bounded, because it guarantees each character participates in only a constant number of word comparisons across all offsets, turning a seemingly expensive search into a linear-in-source scan. I also mention that I would precompute word-to-integer identifiers so the chunk comparisons avoid repeated substring hashing, which matters at gateway throughput, and that the clear-on-unknown-word step is the usual place correctness slips if forgotten. Showing that I reason about both the offset decomposition and the practical hashing cost is what convinces an interviewer I have implemented this for real.
